segments.html: Apply the HUNT modifier to the initial SURVIVAL roll when hunting. In autumn, game is fat and moving in the open. In spring, animals are lean, nursing, and scarce. In summer, thick cover breaks sight lines and prey is alert. In winter, snow shows every track but the short day and cold exposure limit what a hunter can do.

Another way to find food during a journey is to hunt. You cannot hike at the same time as you hunt. However, several people can hunt at the same time. If you want to roll separately you cannot hunt in the same location, which means that any mishaps will affect you individually. An option is that one of you hunts and the others help.

You can choose to hunt for one or two Quarters. If you hunt for one Quarter, you hunt for small game. If you hunt for two Quarters, you can hunt for large game. If you hunt for one Quarter, reroll results 5–6 on the hunting table below. If you hunt for two Quarters, reroll results 1–3. Reroll as long as needed to get a different result.
Apply these terrain modifiers to the initial SURVIVAL roll:

• +1 in Plains, Forest, or Marshlands.
  • 0 in Dark Forest, Hills, Quagmire, or Lake/River.
  • -1 in Mountains or Ruins.
itemLiHtmls: • +1 in Plains, Forest, or Marshlands.
• 0 in Dark Forest, Hills, Quagmire, or Lake/River.
• -1 in Mountains or Ruins.

segments.html: If the expanded weather rules are in use, also apply these modifiers:

• Strong Wind: HUNT -1. Animals scatter. Wind kills scent and sound.
  • Drizzle: HUNT -1. Game takes cover. Wet ground is loud underfoot.
  • Downpour: HUNT -2. Rain drowns tracks, sound, and sight. Most prey will not move.
  • Storm: HUNT is not possible this Quarter Day.
  • Active snowfall: The initial SURVIVAL roll gains +1. Fresh tracks stand out in new snow. The kill roll is unaffected.
  • Clear skies in winter: HUNT +1. Frozen ground is quiet and last night's tracks are still legible.
itemLiHtmls: • Strong Wind: HUNT -1. Animals scatter. Wind kills scent and sound.
• Drizzle: HUNT -1. Game takes cover. Wet ground is loud underfoot.
• Downpour: HUNT -2. Rain drowns tracks, sound, and sight. Most prey will not move.
• Storm: HUNT is not possible this Quarter Day.
• Active snowfall: The initial SURVIVAL roll gains +1. Fresh tracks stand out in new snow. The kill roll is unaffected.
• Clear skies in winter: HUNT +1. Frozen ground is quiet and last night's tracks are still legible.

segments.html: Weather, season, and terrain modifiers all stack. A hunter going out in autumn rain in the forest rolls SURVIVAL with +1 (forest) +1 (autumn) -1 (drizzle) = +1. The same hunter in spring downpour in the mountains rolls -1 (mountains) -2 (spring) -2 (downpour) = -5. That roll is almost certainly a failure, which is the point — nobody hunts in a spring mountain storm.

You need some form of gear to hunt - either a ranged weapon or a hunting trap of some type. First, you must find your prey, which you can do by making a SURVIVAL roll (see the MASTER OF THE HUNT and HUNTING INSTINCTS talents in Chapter 4).

Success means that you find some kind of prey. Roll on the table above to see what type of animal it is. If you roll multiple ⚔️, you can reroll on the hunting table once per extra ⚔️. You cannot go back to a previous result.

To kill your prey you must roll again, this time for MARKSMANSHIP (if using a weapon) or SURVIVAL again (if you are using a trap). Modify the roll with the difficulty of the an imal, according to the table. You don’t need to fight the animal, rolling once is enough. Note that some animals cannot be caught with a trap.

The table to the upper left indicates how many units of MEAT and PELTS your prey yields. The MEAT can be cooked by a CHEF or at an INN, and is then turned into an equal amount of FOOD. You can eat MEAT raw — you then consume a unit of MEAT instead of rolling your Resource Die for FOOD. The PELTS can be turned into LEATHER by a TANNER, preferably at a TANNERY.

MEAT AND SPOILAGE. How long raw MEAT keeps depends on temperature. In summer heat (HEAT 3 or higher), raw MEAT must be eaten or cooked before the end of the current Quarter Day. In normal conditions, MEAT keeps for one day. In winter cold (HEAT 0 or lower), raw MEAT keeps for D3 days before it spoils. A successful CHEF roll during MAKE CAMP extends any MEAT by one extra day — this requires a TINDERBOX. These spoilage times also apply to raw FISH.

If your first SURVIVAL roll fails, you suffer a mishap. Roll on the table to the lower left. If your second roll fails to kill your prey, it only means you don’t get the FOOD – unless it is a boar, in which case it immediately attacks.
* Boars attack you if you fail.
† Partridge, pigeon, dove, or similar. In Marshlands or next to a lake or river, treat this result as waterfowl (duck, coot, heron) with the same stats.

rows: You fall or twist your ankle and suffer a critical injury, equivalent to results 25-26 in the table for blunt trauma.
You lose some of your hunting gear or a weapon. The GM decides which.
Your clothes are damaged. Your boots break or your robe rips on thorny plants or sharp rocks. You must roll for the effects of cold. Your clothes can be mended by making a successful CRAFTING roll.
You step into another hunter's trap. It could be a snare, a net, or a covered pit. You suffer one point of damage to Strength and must make a MOVE roll to get out of the trap.
A wolf, bear or other wild animal feels threatened, and attacks you. The GM chooses an animal.
You bring down a random animal, but is sick and whoever eats of its flesh is infected by a disease with a Virulence rating of 3. This is discovered during your next meal.

segments.html: If you are in a hexagon by a river or lake or by the ocean you can FISH. If you are on foot, you cannot HIKE while FISHING, but you can FISH from a moving boat. Several people can FISH at the same time. If you want to roll separately you cannot FISH in the same location, meaning that any mishaps will affect you individually. Alternative ly, one of you FISHES and the others help. To FISH, you need fishing gear. Make a SURVIVAL roll modified by the FISHER talent and any Gear Bonus from your fishing gear.

Success means you catch a number of units of FISH equal to the number of ⚔️ you rolled. The FISH can be cooked by a CHEF or at an INN, and is then turned into an equal amount of FOOD. You can eat FISH raw - you then consume a unit of FISH instead of rolling your Resource Die for FOOD. You need to do this within a day, or the FISH will be spoiled. If your roll fails, you don’t catch any FISH and you also suffer a mishap. Roll on the table above. If you use the "Pushed long time rolls" module, you also suffer a mishap if you push and fail to add any ⚔️.

rows: Your hook or net snags on the bottom. You must make aMIGHTroll to be able to retrieve your fishing gear. If you fail, it is lost.
You manage to pierce your own finger with the hook, instead of hooking a fish. You suffer one point of damage toStrength. Reroll if fishing with a net.
Your fishing gear breaks. You need to repair it (aCRAFTINGroll) or get new gear.
A large swarm of mosquitoes or gnats attacks you, driving you crazy with their bites and buzzing. They attack with four Base Dice, causing damage toEmpathy.
You lose your balance and fall into the water. See rules for swimming and drowning.
A vicious fish or eel attacks you, causing a nasty bleeding wound. You suffer one point of damage toStrength.

segments.html: When traveling the lands, you can survey for valuable features of the terrain by spending a Quarter Day in the same hex and making a SCOUTING roll. If you are in a water hex you must have a boat to survey the lands, unless you have the DIVER talent.
If you fail, roll a mishap. If you are in a boat, roll for a Sea Travel mishap; otherwise roll on the table below.

On a success, make a roll for a feature. The GM makes a roll for a complication. You will find tracks or other signs from any complication in time, unless otherwise stated in the complication. A complication will use, guard, or have laid claims to the feature if there is any. Use the feature and complication tables available for this module.

On a pushed success, any complication spots the party before you find any tracks of it. It can choose to ambush the party, or make itself known. A complication can call for aid within the Quarter Day, and may become larger or more organized.
You may not survey the lands while on an Ice Cap or Sea Ice tile. Rivers are scouted with their first nearby hex.

rows: RollSURVIVALeach Quarter Day to be able to leave your current hex.
Your clothes are damaged. Roll for the effects of COLD.
You suffer a critical injury, equivalent to results 25-26 for blunt trauma.
RollHEALING. If you succeed you take 1 Strength damage, otherwise you take 2.
A wolf, bear, crocodile, shark, or other wild animal feels threatened and attacks you.
Something is watching and you feel forced to abandon the survey. For 2D6 days (hidden roll), any successful Survey in this hex allows any complication to ambush you.

segments.html: Next to river or lake (not ocean): Hunt +0. Allows fishing. You may forage water even on a failure, but then everyone doing so must roll against disease with virulence rating 3 unless boiled.

Next to river only: Allows construction of a water mill. Halve the construction time for the moat stronghold location. Irrigation grants a +2 bonus to construct the field and garden stronghold locations.
Lake/Ocean: Hunt +0. Allows fishing. Requires boat or raft.
Plains: Forage -1, Hunt +1.
Forest: Forage +1, Hunt +1. -2 to construct wind mills.

Dark forest: Forage -1, Hunt +0. Difficult terrain. -2 to construct wind mills. Constructing a field, garden, or pasture stronghold location requires warm weather, and a failed roll creates an uncontrolled forest fire that destroys most flammable things in the hex and can spread to adjacent hexes depending on upcoming weather.

Hills: Forage +0, Hunt +0. +2 to construct wind mills. Ramparts or palisades receive an automatic +1 to defense rating. Double construction time to construct a field or garden stronghold location. Wells must be built as cisterns and use 10 times the materials and take months instead of weeks to complete.

Mountains: Forage -2, Hunt -1. Difficult terrain. +2 to construct Quarry. Cannot hold field, garden, fence, or pasture stronghold locations. Ramparts or palisades receive an automatic +1 to defense rating. Wells must be built as cisterns and use 10 times the materials and take months instead of weeks to complete.

Marshlands: Forage +1, Hunt +1. Allows fishing. Requires boat or raft. -1 to construct any stronghold location, except moat. Marshlands are rich hunting ground — waterfowl, otter, and wading birds concentrate in wetland cover. You may forage for purple shells except in winter. Diving requires an ENDURANCE roll at -2 unless you have DIVER. If the temperature is cold, roll for COLD. For each success on a dive, you find a shell worth 6D6 silver and 1 unit of MEAT. A mishap can result in a surprise crocodile attack.

Quagmire: Forage -1, Hunt +0. Difficult terrain. -1 to construct any stronghold location, except moat. A quarry can possibly yield peat instead of stone; the peat is a LIGHT resource and can be used as fuel. If you are a TANNER, you can make a SURVIVAL roll to have the Quagmire function as a root cellar or a tannery. Do this just like if you were constructing the location, but eschew the material costs.

Ruins: Forage -2, Hunt -1. Difficult terrain. -2 to construct the field stronghold location. Counts as a free quarry for stone. When constructing a stronghold location, you only need half the amount of stone, as you can reuse old building blocks.
Ashlands: Any found water will be undrinkable or poisonous. Cannot construct well. Can count as a free quarry for volcanic ash.

Firelands: Forage -2. Forage for water yields poisonous water. Cannot construct well or root cellar. Any activities requiring digging are reduced to half speed and need a roll against an extra Gear Die per week. Any X means the ground yields a flow of semi-molten rock. Roll a Gear Die for each nearby worker; on X they become covered in molten rock. NPCs are automatically killed, while player characters roll for a fire based Critical Injury.
Crimson Forest: Forage +1, Hunt +1. Consuming anything edible or drinkable found comes with the risk of contracting Crimson Sickness.

Tundra: Forage -1, Hunt +1. Cannot hold field, garden, fence, or pasture stronghold locations. If you use the "New quarry feature" module, then any found resource is black sand from the Bitter Reach. This cannot be used as normal sand, like to make glass, but 4 units can be made into 1 unit of Iron on a successful CRAFTING roll by a SMITH. A quarry here also has a high chance of finding peat.
Ice Cap: Hunt -1. Difficult terrain, unless snowshoes, skis, or sled.
Beneath the ice: Difficult terrain.
Ice Forest: Forage -1, Hunt +0. Counts as a free quarry for Stone (petrified wood). Cannot hold the field, garden, fence, or pasture stronghold locations.
Sea Ice: Hunt +0. Very difficult terrain. Snowshoes, skis, sled, or boat can partially help.

When the journey of the day is over, it's time to make camp. Finding a good location for a camp, making a fire, and preparing where to SLEEP takes a whole Quarter Day – usually the Evening. Only one person rolls to MAKE CAMP, but others can help her.

Make a SURVIVAL roll, modified by the QUARTERMASTER talent. If your roll succeeds, you establish a basic camp. A basic camp is enough for a crude fire, rough bedding, and a place to keep your gear together. You can REST and SLEEP there, but it is still a poor camp. It gives no special benefit beyond counting as a camp.
One success buys you the night. The fire is lit and the ground is chosen, the gear is gathered, and the group has enough order to sleep without using the BARE GROUND rules. Nothing more is provided.
Each additional ⚔️ success after the first provides the following:

• Each adventurer can recover 1 additional point in one attribute of their choice when RESTING or SLEEPING in the camp.
  • The camp is well hidden from enemies trying to track the party down. The enemies must succeed at a SCOUTING roll and match or exceed the number of ⚔️ successes of the MAKE CAMP roll. If they do not, a camp encounter is averted.
  • Choose one camp improvement from the list below. The same improvement cannot be chosen more than once.
itemLiHtmls: • Each adventurer can recover 1 additional point in one attribute of their choice when RESTING or SLEEPING in the camp.

• The camp is well hidden from enemies trying to track the party down. The enemies must succeed at a SCOUTING roll and match or exceed the number of ⚔️ successes of the MAKE CAMP roll. If they do not, a camp encounter is averted.
• Choose one camp improvement from the list below. The same improvement cannot be chosen more than once.

segments.html: If your roll fails, your camp is less pleasant. You still set up a camp where you can REST and SLEEP, but the GM makes a hidden roll on the failed camp table below. The result is a liability in the camp: a weakness that matters when the night is tested by cold, weather, watch duty, gear handling, food, water, or sudden danger.

The Night is divided into watches as the group sees fit. Up to three adventurers can divide the Night between them and each take one watch. A single adventurer can stand more than one watch, but if they have not SLEPT during the last six Quarter Days of the day, they become SLEEPY at the end of the Night Quarter. That adventurer can SLEEP during some other Quarter Day, usually the Evening.

A normal campfire gives full fire and light through the first full watch after the camp is made. After that, it gives only half fire and half light distance through later watches unless someone tends it or an improvement says otherwise.
Each camp improvement lasts until you break camp.

rows: Your campfire is well built and shielded. A normal campfire gives full fire and light through the first watch, then only half fire and half light distance through later watches. A banked fire keeps full fire and light until the end of the REST.
You have rigged branches, hides, or canvas against the weather. The camp counts as having a tent for the night. Clothes, bedding, and sensitive gear are not soaked by ordinary night rain or snow.
You have kept the sleepers off the cold ground. Everyone in the camp counts as having a sleeping fur during REST and SLEEP.

Stones, fuel, and hanging space are laid out properly. A CHEF gets +2 when preserving meat or fish during camp. If no CHEF is present, cooked fresh meat or fish keeps until the end of the next Day even in hot conditions.

You have chosen a proper sentry place with a clear approach. The lookout gets +1 to SCOUTING rolls while KEEPING WATCH over the camp. If a night threat is spotted, the party is awake in time and is not surprised.

Firelight is low, gear is muffled, and the camp is tucked away. Ordinary camp noise such as talking, cooking, eating, tending gear, or light crafting does not by itself reduce the camp's concealment. Even loud, extended, or reckless campbound activity counts only as normal camp noise unless it would plainly be heard or seen at a distance.

Mounts and pack animals are secured and placed properly. They do not scatter from ordinary night fright, noise, or weather. The lookout also gets +1 to SCOUTING against threats approaching through the animals' side of camp.
The camp is open and badly placed. Enemies trying to find the camp get +2 to SCOUTING.
The fire sits badly and the smoke hangs low. Enemies trying to find the camp get +1 to SCOUTING, and the lookout gets -1 to SCOUTING against approaching threats.
Weather turns to overnight rain or snowfall. Everyone in the camp must roll against COLD as normal for the weather. Clothes, bedding, and sensitive gear are soaked unless the camp has Dry Shelter.
The camp is cluttered and badly laid out. The first time an adventurer needs a specific item during the night, it takes one extra round to find and ready it.
The fire is weak or badly placed. It drops to half fire and half light distance immediately after the first watch.
The sleep is poor and the ground fights the body. No adventurer recovers Agility from the REST.

The camp is filthy and the sleepers wake with dirty dressings, inflamed cuts, and grime worked into every scrape. No adventurer recovers Strength from the REST. If you use the HYGIENE rules, each adventurer's Hygiene Die is reduced by one step.

Food, bedding, and skin are plagued by pests. Everyone in the camp must roll their food Resource Die twice during the night. If you use the HYGIENE rules, each adventurer's Hygiene Die is reduced by one step.
The camp carries in the dark. If a nearby threat has any reason to search for the party during the night, it gets +2 to SCOUTING and cannot be kept away by ordinary camp noise discipline.
The bad camp turns active. Roll on the Trouble at Camp table below.
A wolf, bear or other wild animal feels threatened, and attacks you. The GM chooses an animal.
A randomly selected adventurer has lost a piece of gear. The GM decides what was lost, and if it can be found.
An item belonging to a randomly selected adventurer is broken. The GM decides what item it is. The item can be repaired with aCRAFTINGroll.

Suddenly, the flames from your campfire spread out of control. Tents, sleeping furs, or other nearby gear catch fire. Each adventurer suffers an attack with five Base Dice, Weapon Damage 1. Each adventurer must also make aMOVEroll to save their gear. Failure means that one piece of equipment, chosen by the GM, is lost in the fire.

segments.html: Resting by the campfire is a good opportunity to recover from damage. If your rest is interrupted by something dramatic, like combat or other similar activity, your activity during the Quarter Day no longer counts as REST.
While you REST, you may also spend XP as long as you are not acquiring new talents or spells. If you want to acquire a new skill this way, you must have successfully used it during the session.

Once per Quarter Day, and at any time during that Quarter Day, you may take a 15-minute short break. You may take this short break even if you perform some other activity that uses up that whole Quarter Day; it will not affect that action.
During a short break, you may roll resource dice to restore attributes, see below. No attribute can be restored more than 1 point during a short break.

Restore 1 Strength: Roll a resource die for food or alcohol (beer, ale, mead, wine, or liquor). Note that while alcohol can be used to restore Strength this way, you need to consume a full resource on purpose for it to have any effect on staving off HUNGER.
Restore 1 Agility: Roll a resource die for water. Note that while undistilled alcohol can be treated as a water resource for avoiding thirst, it will not restore Agility.
Restore 1 Empathy: Roll a resource die for liquor, or rank 3 Chef food/alcohol.
Restore 1 Wits: Roll a resource die for tobacco.
Restore 1 Willpower: Roll a resource die for narcotics. Cannot restore Willpower above the Potency of the narcotics; common narcotics might have a base potency of 2.

If you don't use the new stronghold functions modules, like that for "Brewery", then you need some other source for these. These recreational drugs work well together with the "Short break" module, but it does not require it.

Becoming intoxicated: Whenever you roll a resource die to take some sips from alcoholic beverage or use narcotics, you must roll a successful ENDURANCE roll, or become INTOXICATED for a Quarter Day. You may on purpose roll extra resource dice, each then requiring an extra X on the ENDURANCE roll. Or you may consume a whole resource die without rolling it, to automatically become INTOXICATED.

Beer/Ale/Mead/Wine: These resources can be used instead of water to quench thirst. If it tastes good and not poor, then it also restores Empathy, just like if a rank 3 CHEF had made food. See INTOXICATED.

Liquor: Can be used as a resource die to restore Empathy, just like if a rank 3 CHEF had made food. If you use the "Add resource die to rolls" module, it can also be used as a resource die when performing a HEALING roll to save a life. See INTOXICATED.
Tobacco: No effect, unless you use the "Short break" module.
Narcotics: See Becoming intoxicated above. Otherwise, no effect, unless you use the "Short break" or the "Apothecary" talent module.

New Condition: INTOXICATED When you use an alcohol or narcotics resource, you can become INTOXICATED, see Becoming intoxicated above. If you become INTOXICATED while already INTOXICATED, you break your Agility and begin to vomit uncontrollably. Being INTOXICATED has several effects:

• Each time you become INTOXICATED, take 1 Agility damage.
  • Take a -2 penalty to all skills.
  • Always roll your full dice pool, even if your attributes have been reduced by damage.
  • After a Quarter Day, remove INTOXICATED.
itemLiHtmls: • Each time you become INTOXICATED, take 1 Agility damage.
• Take a -2 penalty to all skills.
• Always roll your full dice pool, even if your attributes have been reduced by damage.
• After a Quarter Day, remove INTOXICATED.

segments.html: Note: If you use the INTOXICATED condition, it synergizes with the "Solid drinker" talent. Also note that rolling your full dice pool while INTOXICATED means you still roll all Agility dice, even though you did take that damage. You are likely still at a loss though, since skills are reduced by 2.
• If you do not use the Inventor talent module, you may substitute this for another talent, like Chef.
itemLiHtmls: • If you do not use the Inventor talent module, you may substitute this for another talent, like Chef.

segments.html: If you have the XP and a teacher, you can learn a new talent, a new skill, a new magical path, or increase a magical path. Without a teacher, you need a WITS roll to learn a new talent or a new path. If you use the "Wits to learn magic" module, all rolls to learn magical paths or spells are made with a penalty equal to the rank you try to attain.
Things that take a full day to craft use two Quarter Days.
You can attempt to repair up to three items in a Quarter Day.

You have to sleep at least one Quarter Day per day (usually during the Night) to avoid becoming sleepy. If your sleep is interrupted by something dramatic, like combat or other similar activity, your activity during the Quarter Day no longer counts as sleep. sleep also counts as rest.

It is possible to sleep in the wilderness without making camp - you simply find a suitable tree to sleep under. You save the time it takes to make camp, but everyone in the group must make a SURVIVAL roll to find a good spot to sleep. Failure means the individual doesn't sleep at all, and thus becomes sleepy. Since you don't have a fire to keep the cold away, you all also suffer the effects of cold.
At HEAT 0 or lower, sleeping on bare ground automatically fails ENDURANCE rolls made to avoid becoming COLD.

In the Ravenlands, survival is gritty and intimate. Mud cakes your boots, smoke clings to your hair, and weeks on the road leave more than calluses behind. The Hygiene Die makes that lived-in hardship matter without bogging the table down, turning grime into a tangible pressure you can feel in the story.

This rule sharpens the campaign's flavor by rewarding small mercies: a bath at an inn, a clean shirt hung by the fire, a barber's quick trim before a tense parley. It nudges play toward the kind of hard, human choices the setting thrives on - whether to spend coin on comfort or save it for steel.
Roll your hygiene die once per day. It can also be directly lowered by very unhygienic actions. If it becomes zero, you become FILTHY.

You may regain your Hygiene die, up to a maximum of a D12 die (or 4D6 if you use the "Xd6 as resources" module), by taking the actions listed below. In general, you cannot take the same hygiene restoration action again, until you have lost at least one hygiene die.

Wash your clothes: +1 hygiene die. Add another +1 hygiene die if you use soap or if you pay 5 copper for a professional washing. Wet clothes need a Quarter Day to hang dry or by a fire in order to dry.
Take a bath: +1 hygiene die. If you do it during a summer or pay 3 copper for a bath at an inn, you avoid becoming cold from taking it. Add another +1 hygiene die if you use soap.
Haircut: +1 hygiene die. Includes beard trim. Costs 5 copper.
Apply perfume: +1 hygiene die. Likely not available if you don't use the "Inventor" module.
Sleep at an inn: No added hygiene dice, but the basic hygienic actions you may take there is enough to not have to roll your hygiene die at the end of the day.

New Condition: FILTHY If you use the "Hygiene" die, then as soon as you lose all your Hygiene die, you become FILTHY. Otherwise, your GM could perhaps give you the FILTHY condition from certain events. Like falling into a pile of manure? Or sleeping in the gutter after a too heavy night out? Being FILTHY has several effects:

• You both smell and look awful. Take a -2 penalty to all MANIPULATION rolls against targets that aren't FILTHY.
  • Whenever you are BROKEN from loss of STRENGTH or AGILITY, you must roll against disease with a virulence rating of 4.
  • As soon as you can wash yourself and your clothes (or in other ways regain a Hygiene die, if you use the "Hygiene" module), you are no longer FILTHY, but any contracted diseases stay.
itemLiHtmls: • You both smell and look awful. Take a -2 penalty to all MANIPULATION rolls against targets that aren't FILTHY.
• Whenever you are BROKEN from loss of STRENGTH or AGILITY, you must roll against disease with a virulence rating of 4.
• As soon as you can wash yourself and your clothes (or in other ways regain a Hygiene die, if you use the "Hygiene" module), you are no longer FILTHY, but any contracted diseases stay.

segments.html: When you stop at an adventure site to EXPLORE it, your journey is interrupted. EXPLORING an adventure site can take anything from a Quarter Day up to several days or even weeks. Sometimes, you might have to take a break to REST or SLEEP while EXPLORING. You cannot REST or SLEEP during the same Quarter as you EXPLORE.
If you have access to a boat or raft, you can cross a river without using a bridge or a ford. You can also travel along a river, across a lake or on an ocean.

Travel by sea works like journeys on land, but with some differences. Instead of a pathfinder, a boat has a skipper, who LEADS THE WAY (roll for SURVIVAL modified by the SAIL or talent) in each new hexagon. Failure takes you into the new hexagon anyway, but you must make a roll on the mishap table.

rows: You sail off course and make no progress on the map during this Quarter Day.
A sudden squall makes your boat tilt suddenly. One important item falls into the water. The GM decides what it is.

Your boat is caught in a whirlpool. The skipper must make aSURVIVALroll (modified by theSAILORtalent). Failure means the boat runs aground and has to be repaired (aCRAFTINGroll) before your journey can continue.

Your boat springs a leak and takes on water. The leak must be repaired (aCRAFTINGroll), which takes one turn (15 minutes), but your journey can continue while you do so. If the leak is not repaired, the boat sinks after D6 hours.
Someone in the group (GM's choice) falls overboard after a large wave hits the boat. See rules for swimming and drowning.
Your boat runs aground and must be abandoned or repaired with aCRAFTINGroll. The boat must be on the shore to be repaired.

segments.html: In the Forbidden Lands, fame does not travel the way light does. It does not fill the land evenly. It follows roads, rivers, trade wagons, and the mouths of people who have reason to repeat a name. A fellowship that slays a troll outside Weatherstone may be celebrated at the inn there for years, yet remain utter strangers to a village three hexes away through marshland where no one trades.

Reputation is tracked locally. Each settlement, stronghold, or trade circle can have its own Reputation score for the fellowship. In most cases, the GM tracks Reputation for the group, not for each adventurer separately, unless one character has become genuinely distinct in a given place.

Alongside Reputation, each place or circle may also carry a Standing score for the fellowship. Reputation measures how well known you are. Standing measures what people think of you. The two are separate. You can be famous and hated, or unknown and quietly trusted.
Reputation is a non-negative score rolled as D6, just like other meaningful dice pools in the game. A local Reputation should usually range from 0 to 10, though legendary cases can climb higher.

rows: A few have heard the name
Known by rumor in the local area or circle
Very hard to ignore in that sphere

segments.html:
CIRCLES OF REPUTATION

Settlement Reputation covers the places the fellowship has touched, but the same system works for any group, faction, or circle the GM wants to track. Peddlers and caravan folk, smiths, ferrymen, mercenaries, shrine-keepers, a thieves' guild in the capital, a holy order that watches the barrow roads — any of these can carry their own Reputation and Standing for the fellowship.

There are no separate rules for these circles. Use Settlement Reputation as the model: a score rolled as D6, a Standing from -3 to +3, and the same distance and rumor logic. The GM decides which circles exist, how far their gossip carries, and when a circle's internal reputation bleeds into a settlement's. A fellowship famous among caravan folk may find that a trading post already knows their name, because the same merchants drink at the same inn.

Track only the circles that matter in your campaign. If the fellowship never deals with river traders, there is no score to keep. If they spend three sessions bargaining with dwarven masons, that circle has earned a line in the notebook.

Standing tracks trust, goodwill, resentment, fear, or hatred. It is not rolled by itself. It modifies what successful Reputation means, and it can affect MANIPULATION, prices, favors, recruitment, and other social outcomes.

This split means you can be high Reputation and low Standing (famous but feared), low Reputation and high Standing (unknown to most but trusted by the few who matter), or any other combination. That is exactly what the world needs.
The GM tracks Reputation only where the fellowship has actually left a mark.

Settlement Reputation. Each village, town, temple-hold, mine camp, or ferry crossing can have its own Reputation score for the fellowship. This is the score rolled when the group arrives, asks for favors, or tries to see how much of its story has taken root.
Settlement Standing. Tracked separately for settlements that matter. A village may know you well and still despise you.

Stronghold Reputation. Each stronghold keeps its own Reputation score, as described in Chapter 9. That score radiates outward by distance and travel routes rather than attaching directly to the adventurers. A keep is known first by nearby villages, road traffic, hirelings, and rivals. Its banner and walls often travel farther than the faces behind them.

EXAMPLE: LOCAL REPUTATION IN PLAY

The fellowship clears a grave-cairn near Pelgreve and kills the ash-wight that had been taking children from the sheep paths. Pelgreve gains Settlement Reputation 4 for the fellowship and Settlement Standing +2. That is enough that their names are plainly known there, and a roll can often yield more than a single ⚔️.

Later they fund a new palisade gate, pay fair wages, and buy winter grain locally instead of stripping the stores bare. Standing rises to +3 and Reputation climbs to 5. Now the name opens doors.

But three hexes south, in a farming hamlet with no road to Pelgreve, nobody has heard of them at all. They are strangers there, and the gate-guard treats them like strangers.

Before anyone cares who you are, they care what they see coming down the road. That matters even more in the Ravenlands, where a village may have heard nothing of you at all, yet still must decide whether to open the gate, set a pot on, or string bows behind the palisade.

Each settlement has a Hospitality score. This is not the same as Standing. Standing reflects what a place thinks of you once it knows you. Hospitality reflects how that place tends to treat unknown travelers on first sight.

rows: Closed, frightened, hungry, or bitter. Strangers are a threat.
Wary and guarded. Outsiders are admitted reluctantly.
Ordinary caution. Strangers are judged case by case.
Open-handed by local standards. Travelers are usually heard out.
Warm, trade-minded, or proud of good hosting.

segments.html: Hospitality can change faster than Reputation or Standing. Bad harvests, raids, plague, holy days, or a hard winter can shift it between visits.

If the settlement is a stronghold or fortified manor, use its Chapter 9 functions when judging Hospitality. An INN, MARKETPLACE, TEMPLE, BRIDGE, ROAD, PIER, and TOWN HALL push Hospitality toward openness if they are staffed and the place lives by traffic. RAMPARTS, PALISADE, GUARD TOWER, DITCH, MOAT, DRAWBRIDGE, and PORTCULLIS do not make a place hostile, but they mean strangers are handled at the gate, not at the hearth. DUNGEON, GALLOWS, TORTURE CHAMBERS, or a history of slave-taking leave a place well known but cold.
When the fellowship arrives at a settlement, a first impression roll is needed only in these cases:

• First visit. The fellowship has never been to this settlement before, or has no local Reputation here.
  • Long absence at low Reputation. A full season or more has passed since the last visit and the fellowship's local Reputation is 2 or lower. People forget strangers quickly.
  • Changed faces. The fellowship's composition has changed so much that the locals would not recognize the group — most of the original members left, or the group is entirely different people carrying the same name.
itemLiHtmls: • First visit. The fellowship has never been to this settlement before, or has no local Reputation here.
• Long absence at low Reputation. A full season or more has passed since the last visit and the fellowship's local Reputation is 2 or lower. People forget strangers quickly.

• Changed faces. The fellowship's composition has changed so much that the locals would not recognize the group — most of the original members left, or the group is entirely different people carrying the same name.

segments.html: If none of these apply, skip straight to the recognition procedure. The settlement already knows what to expect.

One character makes the first impression roll. This is usually MANIPULATION, but the group may instead roll the most relevant local Reputation if they are openly leaning on a name already known there.
The roll happens before recognition. It answers a simpler question: do the locals hear you out, let you near the hearth, keep hands off weapons, or put hands on them.
Apply the settlement's Hospitality as a modifier to the roll. Then apply presentation modifiers.

rows: Clean appearance: washed, barbered, or recently lodged at an inn
Useful burden or news: medicine, grain, hunted meat, a message, captured raiders, or a wounded villager brought home alive
Respectful approach: weapons sheathed, helms off, hands visible, asking leave before entry
FILTHY, or visibly foul and unwashed
Heavily armed, blood-spattered, dragging prisoners, or plainly dangerous
Threatening posture, shouted demands, crowding the gate, or visible siege gear

segments.html: Some of these shift by context. A starving hamlet may mistrust rich strangers. A village plagued by beasts may welcome armed help that would unnerve a market town.

rows: Shut out, watched, overcharged, or told to wait outside while authority is fetched.
Heard out, but with caution. Locals remain guarded.
Admitted without much fuss. Folk treat the group as hard travelers rather than immediate threat.
Welcomed promptly, offered guidance, and treated as guests worth dealing with.

segments.html: This roll does not replace Reputation. It establishes the mood before recognition, and it matters most when the fellowship is still unknown.

If a settlement has a palisade, ramparts, a guarded bridge, or a gate shut against danger, the first impression roll also decides whether the gate opens. In such places, the first conversation happens through a gate hatch, from a tower, or over sharpened stakes. That should be a real moment in play.

• If the fellowship has local Standing +1 and Settlement Reputation 2 or higher, no gate roll is needed during ordinary daylight hours.
  • If Standing is +2 or higher, or the group is expected or carrying a recognized token of authority, no gate roll is needed unless the settlement is under alarm.
  • Otherwise, the spokesperson rolls the first impression.
itemLiHtmls: • If the fellowship has local Standing +1 and Settlement Reputation 2 or higher, no gate roll is needed during ordinary daylight hours.
• If Standing is +2 or higher, or the group is expected or carrying a recognized token of authority, no gate roll is needed unless the settlement is under alarm.
• Otherwise, the spokesperson rolls the first impression.

segments.html: A PALISADE or RAMPARTS justifies a real gate encounter. If the place also has a DITCH or MOAT, plus a DRAWBRIDGE or PORTCULLIS, stricter terms are natural even when the locals are not hostile.

rows: Gates stay shut. The group is questioned from outside, told to camp beyond the ditch, or refused entry until a local authority arrives.
Admitted narrowly: peace-bonded weapons, one spokesperson inside, stabling outside the wall, or a guard escort.
The gate opens under ordinary caution. The group may enter and seek the inn, shrine, chief, or market.
Quick admission. Guards point the group toward lodging, the headman, or whoever ought to hear their business.

segments.html: If Standing is negative, even a successful gate opening may come with conditions: weapons stacked at the gate, hostages or sureties, a watchful escort, or denial of entry after dark.

EXAMPLE: FIRST IMPRESSION AND GATE

The fellowship reaches a hilltop fort with a PALISADE and GUARD TOWER. The place has Hospitality 0 and the group has no local Reputation. Garmelda speaks for the group. She rolls MANIPULATION with the Hospitality modifier of 0. She is clean from the inn at the last crossroads (+1) and the group carries fresh venison and word of a bandit camp on the north road (+1). But they are heavily armed and blood is still crusted on Tyrgar's mail (-1). Net modifier: +1.

She rolls 2 ⚔️. The guards open the gate under ordinary caution and point them toward the inn. If she had rolled no swords at all, the group would be sleeping outside the ditch tonight.
The same arrival logic supports other situations without extra burden.

• Night arrival. Most settlements worsen Hospitality by -1 or -2 after dark unless the group is expected or already trusted.
  • Season and hunger. In famine, plague, or siege, rich appearance may provoke fear or envy as often as respect.
  • Sponsor rule. If a known resident, guild contact, priest, or caravan master vouches for the group, use the sponsor's Standing for the first impression. Switch back to the group's own scores once the introduction is complete.
  • Peace-bonding weapons. Some villages admit armed strangers only if bows are unstrung, shields stacked, and long weapons tied at the gate.

• Season and hunger. In famine, plague, or siege, rich appearance may provoke fear or envy as often as respect.

• Sponsor rule. If a known resident, guild contact, priest, or caravan master vouches for the group, use the sponsor's Standing for the first impression. Switch back to the group's own scores once the introduction is complete.
• Peace-bonding weapons. Some villages admit armed strangers only if bows are unstrung, shields stacked, and long weapons tied at the gate.

segments.html: Once the fellowship is through the gate — or at least not turned away at the fence — the question shifts from "do we let them in?" to "who are they?"
When the fellowship enters a settlement and has reason to be recognized, follow this order.
Step 1: Roll Settlement Reputation. Roll a number of D6 equal to the fellowship's local Settlement Reputation there. Each ⚔️ means recognition.

• 1 ⚔️: a few people know the name or deed.
  • 2 ⚔️: the group is known by the right people or by much of the settlement.
  • 3+ ⚔️: the fellowship's name carries real weight here.
itemLiHtmls: • 1 ⚔️: a few people know the name or deed.
• 2 ⚔️: the group is known by the right people or by much of the settlement.
• 3+ ⚔️: the fellowship's name carries real weight here.

segments.html: Standing then determines whether that recognition is warm, wary, fearful, or bitter.
If local Settlement Reputation is 0, move to the next step.
Step 2: Check Stronghold Reputation. If the fellowship owns or rules a nearby stronghold, use that stronghold's Reputation with distance penalties.

rows: Usually no effect unless strong routes or major rumor sources apply

segments.html: If a road, river, or caravan route directly links the stronghold and the settlement, the GM may ignore 1 point of distance penalty. A ROAD built from the stronghold, a BRIDGE over the local river, or a PIER that ties the place into traffic should count as such a link — not just as flavor.

Roll the effective score as D6. Success means people know the keep, its banner, or the people tied to it. If this recognition keeps repeating in the same settlement, start converting it into permanent local Settlement Reputation instead of rolling the stronghold every time.

Step 3: Check Circle Reputation. If the settlement includes people from a circle the fellowship has touched — a trade, a guild, a faction — roll the fellowship's Reputation in that circle. This does not mean the whole village knows them. It means the people of that circle might. If those contacts speak of the fellowship locally over time, some of that recognition can become Settlement Reputation.

Step 4: Check Rumor Sources. If an active rumor has reached the hex, the GM can either roll its strength directly as D6 or simply treat it as already having granted local Reputation there. The second method is usually better once a rumor has settled into local memory.
KIN: If the settlement is primarily populated by another kin than your own, your effective Reputation score counts as two steps lower.

THE GROUP: When an entire fellowship arrives, do not roll for each PC. Roll once, using the fellowship's shared local Reputation. If one adventurer is individually famous there, the GM may roll for that character separately.
NPCs can also have local Reputation scores. Roll the same way to determine whether the fellowship has heard of an NPC before meeting them.

In the Ravenlands, a name that carries weight is worth more than silver. When fighters and killers have earned enough scars, enough victories, enough stories told around fires in places that matter, their name alone can open a warchief's hall, silence a crowded inn, or make a guard step aside without drawing steel. These are people whose deeds have been spoken of so many times that the name itself has become a thing — a weapon, a key, a warning.
When dealing with a place or circle where you have local Reputation, you may lean on your name. Roll the relevant Reputation score. The GM interprets ⚔️ according to context.

rows: Fair hearing, access, basic hospitality, reduced suspicion.
Minor favor, quick introduction, small credit, modest price break, useful rumor.
Significant favor, audience with authority, meaningful local help, strong deference.
The kind of response that shapes a scene: public backing, a chief's own table, rare privilege, or a concession no stranger would receive.

segments.html: Standing modifies the outcome. Where your Standing is good, your name is a gift. Where your Standing is foul, that same name may clear a room — but not in your favor. Fear, resentment, or hostile attention follow a hated name as surely as respect follows a loved one.

A name is not permanent. It must be fed with deeds, or it fades. And a name that grows too large for its Standing draws the wrong kind of attention: rivals who want to test it, enemies who want to end it, and common folk who would rather not be near when the reckoning comes.

EXAMPLE: LEANING ON YOUR NAME

The fellowship has Settlement Reputation 5 and Standing +2 in Pelgreve. They need horses for a hard ride south. Heme rolls five dice and gets 2 ⚔️. The stable-master offers two good mounts on credit because the fellowship's word is sound here. If Standing were -1 instead, the stable-master might still know the name — but he would charge double and watch them ride out with a hand on his purse.
When you MANIPULATE someone, the local Reputation and Standing scores can apply. Use whichever combination matters most:

• Use Standing as the modifier to the social contest when trust or resentment is the question.
  • Use Reputation to determine whether the target knows who you are and whether your name can be leaned on.
  • Use Hospitality for first meetings, gates, lodging, and the settlement's instinctive treatment of unknown travelers.
itemLiHtmls: • Use Standing as the modifier to the social contest when trust or resentment is the question.
• Use Reputation to determine whether the target knows who you are and whether your name can be leaned on.
• Use Hospitality for first meetings, gates, lodging, and the settlement's instinctive treatment of unknown travelers.

segments.html: If your local Reputation is higher than your target's, you get a +1 modification to your roll. If your local Reputation is more than double theirs, you get +2. If the target's is higher, they get the same bonus. Read more about MANIPULATION in Chapter 5.
When a deed becomes widely talked about, it creates a rumor source. The source begins in a settlement, stronghold, road station, caravan, or adventure site tied to the event.
Each rumor source has a strength (how powerful the story is), a tone (admired, feared, cursed, blessed, disputed), and a sphere (settlement, stronghold, circle, or broader regional).

rows: Minor talk, local memory, road gossip.
Strong local tale, likely to spread through nearby hexes.

segments.html: How fast do rumors travel? In the Ravenlands, most people used to live and die within a day's walk of where they were born. News moves only when someone carries it — a peddler, a drover, a mercenary company, a messenger bird, or an adventurer with a tale and a thirst. There are no town criers, no postal roads, no reliable couriers outside the richest holdings.
As a baseline, check rumor spread whenever the GM advances time by a season or when a significant stretch of weeks (such as a month) has passed. In that time, a rumor source can spread roughly:

• 2-3 hex through trackless wilderness where few travel.
  • 4-9 hexes along a road or river where traders, drovers, or pilgrims move.
  • 10+ hexes if carried by active caravans, mercenary bands, or regular ferry traffic along a well-traveled route.
itemLiHtmls: • 2-3 hex through trackless wilderness where few travel.
• 4-9 hexes along a road or river where traders, drovers, or pilgrims move.
• 10+ hexes if carried by active caravans, mercenary bands, or regular ferry traffic along a well-traveled route.

segments.html: When using Chapter 9 stronghold functions, treat ROAD, BRIDGE, and PIER as the links that improve rumor travel. A staffed INN, MARKETPLACE, or TOLL HOUSE makes stories spread more reliably along that route, because strangers pass through, eat, bargain, gossip, and carry tales onward. DOVECOTE is not mass rumor, but it moves urgent news, claims, threats, and invitations unusually fast between already linked places.

When a rumor reaches a new settlement or circle, it usually adds +1 Reputation there, more if the deed was enormous or repeated, and may shift Standing if the tone strongly favors or damns the fellowship.
Rumors build actual local Reputation scores that can later be rolled. They are not vague awareness. They are the slow accumulation of stories that give a name weight in a place.

SIMPLIFIED RUMOR TRACKING

If you do not want to count hexes and weeks, use this instead. When the fellowship does something worth talking about, ask yourself three questions:

  • Who would carry this story? Traders, hirelings, refugees, soldiers, priests, or travelers who were present or heard it firsthand.
  • Where do those people go? Along roads, rivers, and trade routes. Not into trackless marsh or deep forest unless someone has reason to go there.
  • How long has it been? A few weeks means nearby settlements along connected routes. A full season means the story has had time to reach any place those carriers regularly visit.

Mark the settlements that would reasonably have heard, and +1 Reputation there.
A great deed raises your name where it happened and where the story travels. It does one or more of these:

• Raises Settlement Reputation where the deed happened.
  • Raises Settlement Standing there if the deed truly helped or harmed the locals.
  • Creates or strengthens a rumor source.
  • Raises Stronghold Reputation if the deed defended, enriched, or elevated the keep.
  • Raises Reputation in whatever circles care about it.
itemLiHtmls: • Raises Settlement Reputation where the deed happened.
• Raises Settlement Standing there if the deed truly helped or harmed the locals.
• Creates or strengthens a rumor source.
• Raises Stronghold Reputation if the deed defended, enriched, or elevated the keep.
• Raises Reputation in whatever circles care about it.

segments.html: How much a deed raises Reputation depends on where the score already stands. The higher your name has already climbed, the harder it is to push it further. Folk who already know you well are not as easily impressed by another dead wolf or another sack of grain.

A small deed is a single act of moderate value — killing a beast, delivering a message, donating useful goods. A major deed shapes the settlement's season — lifting a siege, ending a plague, recovering stolen kin. A defining deed is the kind of thing that names a place or an age. At high Reputation, only defining deeds still move the score. Everything else is just living up to what people already expect.
Examples of deeds that grow local Reputation:

• A feared monster was slain near the settlement.
  • The settlement was defended against raiders, undead, or fire.
  • Stolen kin, goods, or livestock were recovered.
  • A prominent NPC was killed or saved from certain death.
  • A legendary treasure or artifact was found.
  • A stronghold function was completed that visibly affects the area.
itemLiHtmls: • A feared monster was slain near the settlement.
• The settlement was defended against raiders, undead, or fire.
• Stolen kin, goods, or livestock were recovered.
• A prominent NPC was killed or saved from certain death.
• A legendary treasure or artifact was found.
• A stronghold function was completed that visibly affects the area.

segments.html: What lowers Standing. Theft, extortion, unpaid debts, humiliating respected locals, cheating in trade, bringing trouble and leaving others to bleed for it, siding with a hated faction, or violating hospitality. Money alone does not buy love. A settlement may respect your silver before it trusts your face.

Stronghold development also feeds into local fame. Completing a Fortress, Castle, or Palace, adding RAMPARTS, opening an INN, cutting a ROAD, building a BRIDGE, or holding games in an ARENA all shape how news of the place spreads. A GALLOWS, DUNGEON, slave-taking, or unpaid hirelings may raise notoriety while poisoning Standing in the settlements that must live under that power.

EXAMPLE: REPUTATION GROWTH AND RUMOR SPREAD

The fellowship raises Black Barrow Keep three hexes from Pelgreve and builds its strength to Stronghold Reputation 6. They cut a ROAD and build a BRIDGE over the local river. Those links mean that nearby settlements hear the name through drovers, messengers, and toll traffic. A village three hexes away might first recognize the banner before it knows the faces behind it. After enough contact, that borrowed recognition becomes local Settlement Reputation of its own.

Meanwhile, the fellowship has Reputation 4 and Standing +1 among caravan folk after protecting wagons and honoring contracts. A ferryman in a distant river-town may know them by name even though the farmers there do not.

But none of that matters at the strange hamlet on the edge of the marshes, where no road runs and no trader calls. There, they are mud-caked strangers rattling the gate at dusk.

Track local Reputation and Standing only for settlements that matter, circles that matter, and strongholds that matter. Do not track the whole map. Track what the fellowship has actually touched. A simple list in a notebook is enough:
When a rumor source expires or a new deed happens, update the list. Nothing else is needed.
A few things worth keeping in mind as the Reputation system runs at your table.

Fame grows slowly. A single performance, a speech in the square, or a round of drinks should not make the fellowship famous. These things spread or reshape a name that already exists. In most cases, a single social scene raises local Reputation by +1 at most. Real fame needs real deeds.

Discounts have limits. If a Peddler's talents already grant strong price reductions, Reputation should not stack another percentage on top. Use the stronger benefit and let the weaker one grant something else: quicker access, first pick of stock, partial credit, or a waived insult premium. The economy should still bite.

Generosity requires means. A starving hamlet does not hand out free rooms and cut-rate smith work because the heroes are loved. It may offer floor space by the hearth, plain food, rumor, or a guide. Reserve the richest hospitality for places that can actually afford it and where Standing is strong enough to justify the favor.

Stronghold fame settles gradually. When the same settlement keeps recognizing the fellowship through stronghold Reputation, convert that into permanent local Settlement Reputation over time — but not all at once. A season of repeated contact is a reasonable pace.

They came down the hill mud-caked and bleeding. Garmelda had a broken rib and Heme had lost his shield somewhere in the marsh. The village gate was shut. The guard looked at them through a slot and said nothing for a long time.

"We killed the thing in the barrow," Garmelda said.

The slot closed. A minute later the gate opened. A woman with grey braids and a belt knife stood there. She looked at the blood, the missing shield, the way the Raven favored her left side.

"You'd better come in," she said. "There's stew. And work, if you want it."
The Reputation system tells the GM how a settlement reacts to the fellowship. What follows tells the players what they can do once they pass through the gate.

Every settlement is a decision point. Time spent inside the walls is time not spent on the road. A fellowship that arrives at dusk must choose: ask around for news, check the notice board for paying work, petition the chief for a favor, trade at the market, drink at the inn, or simply rest. Each of these costs a quarter day, the same as any journey activity. The walls do not stop time from moving.
When the fellowship arrives at a settlement, the visit follows a natural sequence:

• Arrival. First Impression roll, if needed. Gate encounter if fortified.
  • Recognition. See Reputation, above. The settlement decides what it knows about you.
itemLiHtmls: • Arrival. First Impression roll, if needed. Gate encounter if fortified.
• Recognition. See Reputation, above. The settlement decides what it knows about you.

segments.html:
• Quarter-day activities. Each character picks one activity per quarter day: ASK AROUND, SEEK WORK, PETITION, TRADE, REPAIR AND CRAFT, CAROUSE, HEAL, REST, or TRAIN.
  • Work. If the fellowship takes a notice board job or accepts a commission, the work follows standard adventure procedures — travel, combat, social encounters, and return.
  • Return and report. Completing work adjusts Reputation, Standing, and patron level. Payment is collected. The notice board updates.
  • Departure. The fellowship leaves with whatever they gained — gear, information, reputation, silver, or scars.
