Two PCs confront a powerful enemy together. It can be a monster or the commander of the attackers.

segments.html: If your PCs take part in the battle at the stronghold, you can affect the result. Your adventurers provide the stronghold with one point of Defense Rating, regardless of number. Also, your adventurers can be subjected to individual events that are played out using the normal combat rules.

At least once per turn, the GM rolls on the table below. It is up to the GM to decide which PC is affected. Play out personal combats before moving on to the next turn of the larger battle. Note that the event can lead to a PC or NPC being Broken, which in turn can affect Attack or Defense Ratings.

The results in the table should primarily be seen as inspiration and will need to be adapted to the situation. The GM is also allowed to disregard the table and make up her own challenges for her adventurers during the battle at the stronghold.
EXAMPLE

Nirmena's and Tyrgar's stronghold is attacked by some 90 savage orcs led by the chieftain, Geldad. The stronghold has ramparts and 20 guards, which gives a total Defense Rating of 5 (one for the adventurers, +2 for the ramparts and +2 for the guards). The attackers have a battering ram and thus get Attack Rating 7 (5 for the number of attackers, +1 for the ram and +1 for Geldad himself).

In the first turn of the battle, the players roll one X while the GM rolls two. The GM chooses to have 20 orcs be cut down, decreasing the number of remaining attackers to 70 and the Attack Rating to 6. The players choose to have the ramparts damaged and then breached, reducing the Defense Rating to 3.

The first turn is over, and it's time to see what happens to Tyrgar and Nirmena themselves. The GM rolls a five, and lets the event happen to Nirmena. She suddenly finds herself face-to-face with Geldad himself on the ramparts! If she defeats the orc chieftain, she might turn the tide of the battle and save the stronghold from destruction...

If your stronghold is surrounded and besieged, you cannot leave it without being attacked. In this situation, your hirelings cannot buy food and water for themselves - instead, everyone in the castle must consume whatever you have stored in the stronghold. As a general rule, five hirelings need to consume one unit of food per day, or they will become hungry. If you have a well, you all have free access to water even during a siege - if not, you will need to provide water for your hirelings too.
Sieges often hinge on specialized tools. The following equipment can be built and used during sieges and open assaults.
These can help your units climb walls and buildings.
✦ REQUIREMENT: — ✦ RAW MATERIALS: 80 WOOD or 20 GRAPPLING HOOKS and 20 ROPE ✦ TOOLS: Saw and hammer ✦ TIME: 1 day / — ✦ EFFECT: +1 to Attack Rating.
Portable wooden walls, often used by the offenders' crossbowmen and the like, to take cover from enemy projectiles.
✦ REQUIREMENT: The BUILDER talent ✦ RAW MATERIALS: 100 WOOD ✦ TOOLS: Saw and hammer ✦ TIME: 2 days ✦ EFFECT: +1 to Attack Rating as long as you are not out of ammunition.

Battering rams are used to break down stone walls or wooden doors. They often consist of a metal headed wooden log suspended in the air by rope over a canopy made with animal hides, often drenched in water, so it wouldn't be as easy for it to catch fire.

✦ REQUIREMENT: The BUILDER talent ✦ RAW MATERIALS: 20 WOOD, 2 IRON and 5 HIDES ✦ TOOLS: Forge, saw and hammer ✦ TIME: 2 days ✦ EFFECT: +1 to Attack Rating as long as your opponent does not have a DRAWBRIDGE. Does not stack with the bonus from a SIEGE TOWER.

A large tower on wheels. It can work as an access point over the enemy walls, if they do not have a drawbridge. But even if they do, the height makes it suitable to shoot at the defenders from. Usually covered in wet hides to prevent fire.

✦ REQUIREMENT: The BUILDER talent ✦ RAW MATERIALS: 250 WOOD and 20 HIDE ✦ TOOLS: Saw and hammer ✦ TIME: 2 weeks ✦ EFFECT: +2 to Attack Rating or +1 if your opponent has a DRAWBRIDGE. Does not stack with the bonus from a BATTERING RAM.
You dig a tunnel supported with wood under the enemy fortification, then fill it with straw and other burnable material and set it alight, so parts of the enemy's walls collapse.

✦ REQUIREMENT: You must be in a siege during the construction time. Enemy cannot have a MOAT. ✦ RAW MATERIALS: 25 WOOD ✦ TOOLS: Shovel, pickaxe, saw, hammer ✦ TIME: 1 week ✦ EFFECT: Damages the defenders' RAMPARTS or PALISADE, usually just before the combat begins.
A wooden frame, with a tension powered arm ending in a bucket, that slings stones towards enemy fortifications. It can’t reach too far, so must be used in reach of enemy counterfire.

✦ REQUIREMENT: "Torsion weapon" research (made at a library), the BUILDER talent ✦ RAW MATERIALS: 100 WOOD and 5 ROPE ✦ TOOLS: Saw and hammer ✦ TIME: 1 week ✦ AMMUNITION: 10 STONES per turn. For arson attacks, you can use 5 barrels with CHARCOAL. ✦ EFFECT: +1 to Attack Rating as long as you have ammunition and at least 3 stationed attackers.
A sling-based catapult that is driven by a heavy counterweight.

✦ REQUIREMENT: "Trebuchet" research (made at a library), the BUILDER talent ✦ RAW MATERIALS: 200 WOOD, 50 STONE, 10 LEATHER, 10 IRON ✦ TOOLS: Saw and hammer ✦ TIME: 2 weeks ✦ AMMUNITION: Same as a catapult. ✦ REPUTATION: +1 ✦ EFFECT: Works like a catapult, but can be used from a siege. If a defender has a trebuchet, they can spend 1d6 units of fire munitions to destroy an enemy trebuchet before it can be set up.

This weapon kind of looks like a gigantic crossbow placed on a pivoting rest on top of a tower. The limbs are powered by the torsion of a twisted rope. It is considered specialized knowledge and must be researched from a library.

✦ REQUIREMENT: "Torsion weapon" research (made at a library), the BUILDER talent ✦ RAW MATERIALS: Guard tower (consumed), 50 WOOD and 2 ROPE ✦ TOOLS: Saw and hammer ✦ TIME: 1 week ✦ AMMUNITION: 1 unit of ballista bolts per turn. These are 10 times as expensive as regular arrows and takes a week to make. ✦ EFFECT: +1 to Defense Rating as long as you have at least 3 GUARDS stationed here and remain ammunition. A bolt thrower could be used in regular combat, it would then use 1 item die, 1 ammunition die and deal 5 damage on a hit. It counts as a monster attack and thus cannot be parried. It takes 2d6 rounds to reload.

To break a siege, you must sally forth and attack the besiegers. This is very dangerous, as your Defense Rating will be lower - it takes 20 guards instead of 10 to gain a point of Defense Rating, and the ramparts, portcullis, guard tower, and moat functions have no effect. The attackers, for their part, cannot use ladders or battering rams in such a battle on open ground.
These procedures keep stronghold play focused and predictable from week to week.

Stronghold events occur weekly, so hirelings measure time in weeks instead of days. When you hire a hireling, you may hire them for up to 1-7 days, or for any number of weeks. Paying for more than a week in advance is allowed, and if you will be gone for more than a week and don’t have a STEWARD to run things while you are away, these investments can be lost if a stronghold event kills or scares your hirelings away.
When a week begins, immediately gain the resources your hireling would produce for that week. This should be done at the same time as you pay them. It makes keeping count of resources much easier.

If you need to actually use all these resources over the week, then all of them might not be available at once. But if you construct things that take the entire week to build, like a house, it is ok to empty the storage in advance, as the materials will be there when you finish.

As long as your shops set up a stock, ideally around three times the amount they sell per week, you don’t need to be exact, then they are allowed to average their sales over each week into a fixed amount, to ease stronghold management.

Each 6 dice of stronghold reputation simply provide 1 ⚔️ toward weekly sales, round down. If you are some points short or in excess, you can modify the demand to a multiple of 6 by lowering or increasing the sale prices by 5% per missing/excessive point.
You hire a HUNTER, a TANNER, and a HAWKER, and you have a TANNERY and a SHOP. Your stronghold reputation is 6, so your weekly sales roll starts at 1 ⚔️.

The hunter produces 2 MEAT per day and 2 PELT per day. That totals 14 MEAT and 14 PELT per week. The MEAT will spoil daily unless you have a ROOT CELLAR, so you salt and cure 12 MEAT in the SMOKERY and eat the rest. The 14 PELTS go to the tannery. A tanner converts 12 PELTS into 12 LEATHER in one Quarter Day, leaving 2 PELTS for later.

You decide to sell LEATHER and a few finished goods in your SHOP. Leather is a specialized item and a consumable. With 1 ⚔️ per week, you can sell 1 LEATHER per week at full price, or sell faster by lowering the price. You set leather to 70% price, moving two categories toward everyday, and triple your weekly sales for that item. That lets you sell 3 LEATHER per week.

You also craft 2 pairs of BOOTS and 1 SLEEPING FUR. Boots are everyday items and sell easily at 70% price (30 x 0.7 = 21 copper). A sleeping fur is specialized and sells at 70% price (30 x 0.7 = 21 copper) with 1 ⚔️ per week. You keep the remaining LEATHER as stock for next week.
Totals for the week: - 3 LEATHER at 15 copper each = 45 copper - 2 BOOTS at 21 copper each = 42 copper - 1 SLEEPING FUR at 21 copper = 21 copper

Total sales: 108 copper. Weekly wages: 84 copper (6 for a tanner per day + 6 for a hunter per day) x 7 = 84 copper, plus 42 copper for the hawker (6 per day). Net profit: 108 - 126 = -18 copper. You are running at a loss, so you choose to add a second HAWKER and set leather back to full price, or you switch the shop to sell higher value goods for fewer sales.

If your stronghold reputation rises to 12, you gain 2 ⚔️ per week and can sell twice as many items at the same price tier. If it falls to 2, you can lower prices by 20% to keep the same number of weekly customers, or accept fewer sales and keep prices steady.
"Walls hold a night. Land holds a lifetime. The wind will pry at your gates, but the soil will take your children if you do not stake it, seed it, and stand by it. Name the ground, then keep it."

This chapter expands the stronghold rules with territory control, nearby hex development, resource yields, and conflicts between settlements. It is written to stand on its own: if you use these rules, treat them as the default stronghold procedures.

Fields grow where the soil can be worked and the plough can bite; gardens and orchards live or die by water and seasons. Pastures and sheepfolds need grass, fencing, and a herder’s eye, while pigsties thrive only where fodder and shelter can be kept. Mines and quarries are not promises but discoveries: you must find the seam, then keep the tools and workers there.

Rivers and lakes decide what can be fished, and roads decide how far you can feed it. A pier gives the water a place to meet your people; a sawmill drinks from a river to turn wood into planks; a bridge is the difference between a road that looks good on a map and one that carries wagons. Guard towers and ramparts do not create control by themselves - they make your claim visible and hard to ignore.

Use the stronghold functions as written, but let the territory rules describe what land can sustain them and how that land must be held. When a function has stricter requirements in the stronghold chapter, follow those requirements.

Territory is the stronghold's lifeline. A stronghold cannot grow or sustain families without controlled food hexes. Use HOUSING from the stronghold chapter to track how many families live within the walls, then check the controlled hexes needed to feed them.

Treat the hexes around a stronghold as a separate management map, just as you do on journeys. Mark nearby hexes, record which ones are claimed, developed, or contested, and track how each hex is being used. This turns the land around the stronghold into a living frontier instead of a blank backdrop.

The GM is encouraged to use hexes around settlements across the world in the same way. A village with a mill on the river, a quarry in the hills, and a pasture in the lowlands should feel different from one starved down to a single field. Territory conflicts are also ready-made adventure hooks: the forest that feeds two villages, the marsh that breeds bandits, the road a rival insists is theirs. Let those borders create reasons to scout, parley, raid, or defend.
Every civilized settlement has a SETTLEMENT level. Each settlement has an adult population equal to three times the number of Families listed below.

rows: Small Castle, Player (or NPC faction) Stronghold (small or medium, if small 4 Settlement Dice, if medium 5 ~ 6 Dice)

segments.html: Settlement size governs how easy it is to spot or hide a community.

rows: Must be discovered withEXPLOREfor a Quarter Day unless a road leads to it. Can be well hidden; up to two ⚔️ onSCOUTINGare needed to discover it while the partyEXPLORE.

Must be discovered withEXPLOREfor a Quarter Day if there is no road and the settlement uses the environment to remain hidden. It can be slightly hidden; one ⚔️ onSCOUTINGis needed to discover it while the partyEXPLORE, but this is rare since a high vantage point reveals hints.
Hints of a large settlement can be seen across the hex from a good viewing point.
Massive settlements can be seen across the hex from almost any viewing point, and hints can be seen from a nearby hex.

segments.html: Use the following requirements for the total number of Food Hexes (including the home hex) a settlement must control. A Food Hex is a developed hex that yields Food (Farm, Pasture, Fishery in river, lake or ocean hexes).

headers: Family Growth Per Extra Food Hex

segments.html: Each additional Food Hex beyond the requirement supports growth. For every extra Food Hex held for a full year, the settlement can add families equal to the secondary plus value of its scale (as listed in its Families line), representing migration and surplus.

Some stronghold functions require controlled hex with a listed quality. It can be the same hex as the Stronghold, or a nearby hex, or a hex connected with a road. If a prerequisite is not met, the function cannot be built or does not operate.

rows: Grazing land, livestock, and a Herder or Fence; Barn required to feed Winter.
Garden, Orchard, or Forest, plus pigs
Access to wood; a developed Lumber Camp hex satisfies this
Adjacent lake or ocean; Pier doubles output

segments.html: Each Family consumes one unit of HOUSING. Housing is based on the total investment into stronghold buildings: each 100 Wood or 100 Stone provides one HOUSING, as long as those materials are not already supporting a stronghold function. Families can also build their own housing without you providing it. A stronghold that controls fewer than half its required food hexes starts to starve. If starvation lasts more than two Seasons, families begin to leave and the stronghold loses effective HOUSING until stability returns.
Families are baseline households. Residents with higher STATUS represent multiple households in HOUSING terms; when those residents leave or die, reduce effective HOUSING rather than family count.

Families are the unit of long-term labor. A family provides able hands unless it is missing its sole provider. When war, raids, or disasters kill providers, affected families count as one-third of a family until the loss is resolved or the population recovers.
For labor and yields, treat one family team as the same staffing assumption as one hireling. This keeps Seasonal yields aligned with Quarter Day production rates.
When residents are recruited, use the stronghold’s Reputation as the same modifier and benchmark used in the stronghold rules, so population growth tracks the established reputation loop.
If a settlement's family balance collapses (such as during wartime), natural population growth stalls. Recovery usually requires Seasons of stability, mergers, or deliberate immigration.

• When a settlement takes in a new craftsman or tradesman, they usually arrive with their family and count toward the Family limit. These families do not provide able hands or militia drafts.
  • If unskilled labor is required, each family that does not provide a tradesman provides 1.5 able hands (so 2 families provide 3 able workers) toward a project.
  • Each family that has its able men drafted or forcibly moved out of the settlement counts as one-third of a family and does not contribute to population growth.

• If unskilled labor is required, each family that does not provide a tradesman provides 1.5 able hands (so 2 families provide 3 able workers) toward a project.
• Each family that has its able men drafted or forcibly moved out of the settlement counts as one-third of a family and does not contribute to population growth.

segments.html: When a stronghold loses a conflict or suffers a major raid, reduce families as follows:

• Skirmish loss: One family per 20 defenders committed.
  • War loss: One family per 10 defenders committed.
  • Siege loss: One family per 5 defenders committed.
itemLiHtmls: • Skirmish loss: One family per 20 defenders committed.
• War loss: One family per 10 defenders committed.
• Siege loss: One family per 5 defenders committed.

segments.html: Treat these as civilian losses after the stronghold battle is resolved. If the battle system already removed guard units or hirelings, do not remove those again as families. Count 10 guards as one defender unit; if residents are raised, 20 residents count as one defender unit. Families lost this way reduce effective HOUSING and available labor until new families arrive. If the stronghold is starving, double these losses.

When a decision is not made beforehand, the GM can use the SETTLEMENT level to check whether a settlement can teach a skill or talent or provide an uncommon or rare item. Hiring a tutor, seller, or mercenary typically requires a WITS or EMPATHY check and a Quarter Day. The GM may also require MANIPULATION to secure the deal, with proper pay or a worthy cause granting +2 dice.

Skills: When a player asks if a town has a tutor who knows a skill's rank, make a SETTLEMENT check. A tutor for Rank 1 is available even if the roll fails and has no 💀. Each ⚔️ increases the tutor's rank by 1, to a maximum of 5.

Talents: When a player asks if a town has a tutor who knows a talent, make a SETTLEMENT check. If the roll has at least one ⚔️ and fewer than three 💀, a tutor for Rank 1 is available. Spellcasting talents require two ⚔️. Each additional ⚔️ beyond the requirement increases the tutor's rank by 1, to a maximum of 5.

Equipment: When a player asks if a town has a specific item, make a SETTLEMENT check. For each two ⚔️, shift the item's Supply one step easier (Rare -> Uncommon -> Common). Never shift Extremely Rare without a story hook. Then roll availability, as normal. If the item is available, you may use another SETTLEMENT check to set quantity: 0 ⚔️ means one item, 1-2 ⚔️ means small stock (up to a dozen), 3+ ⚔️ means plentiful (up to a hundred). Individual quantities raise asking price by 25%, while plentiful items allow the seller to provide discounts about 10% to buyers of high REPUTATION or when buying bulk. The GM should note the result and keep it for a month or two before rerolling.

When the party asks to find a henchman or mercenary, use the number of Families to determine availability. If you have adult population data (excluding children under 13), divide by 3 to estimate Families. Divide the Families by the ratio below for each type sought to determine how many are available for hire. Track those hired or lost to events.

Classes are rarer and more independent. They are not simply better, but harder to hire unless the cause aligns with their ideals. They do not ask for monthly pay but for a share of the wealth, discovery, or a cause.
Availability ratios are local and seasonal. War, famine, festivals, or rumors can shift a ratio band by one step at the GM's discretion.

The ratios below also include kin ratios in human settlements. Use the highest ratio between the NPC/Class and the kin when players seek a specific kin. The GM decides when a kin is not present at all. Local history can override kin ratios. A dwarven mine town or an Aslene trading post may break the default balance.

Hunter (many able men double as hunters)
Guard/Militia, Bandit, Thief, Simple Craftsman (carpenter, builder)
Soldier/Army, Rider, Hunter Class, Rogue Class, Other Human Nations
Fighter Class, Rider Class, Halfling kin
Trader, Minstrel, Craftsman Expert (blacksmith, healer/alchemist), Dwarf kin

Priest, Sorcerer, Minstrel Class, Peddler Class

segments.html: Veteran availability multiplies the ratios. These veterans are limited and non-replenishable until the end of each even year.
If the job involves open conflict, cursed sites, or known horrors, increase pay by 25% without a roll.
If the hireling must travel more than one hex to reach the stronghold, add 1-2 days of travel before they can begin work.

Hunter (many able men double as hunters)
Guard/Militia, Bandit, Thief, Simple Craftsman (carpenter, healer)

segments.html: Base daily pay is usually prepaid for a week. Hirelings may negotiate for higher pay in high-risk periods (no more than twice, and only for that event) or for a share of treasure (a typical contract shares 1/5 of sold finds among hirelings who took the risk).

When hiring in larger settlements, roll a SETTLEMENT check. For each ⚔️ beyond the first, the hireling asks for 10% more pay (rounded down). On a failure, they are going through hard times and may accept lower pay after a successful MANIPULATION roll. The GM should only make this roll occasionally, such as once per month. During winter or severe hardship, hirelings ignore one ⚔️ success on this roll.
Every hex around a stronghold falls into one of four states:

• Wild: No permanent influence. Bandits, monsters, and weather rule the hex.
  • Claimed: A settlement asserts control, but the land is still untamed.
  • Developed: The land is worked and guarded. It yields steady resources.
  • Contested: Two or more powers struggle for control.
itemLiHtmls: • Wild: No permanent influence. Bandits, monsters, and weather rule the hex.
• Claimed: A settlement asserts control, but the land is still untamed.
• Developed: The land is worked and guarded. It yields steady resources.
• Contested: Two or more powers struggle for control.

segments.html: Each claimed or developed hex has a Control Score from 0 to 6. Control measures patrols, infrastructure, population ties, and fear.

Territory actions are political and labor-intensive. Each action requires families committed for a full Season to succeed. One hex is 10 kilometers wide; clearing, fencing, hauling, and patrolling take time and people.

Use the commitment table below as a baseline. Relevant stronghold functions make work more efficient and reduce the families required by 1 (minimum 1). After committing families, roll the SETTLEMENT dice pool; each ⚔ reduces the required families by 1 (minimum 1). If the roll shows no ⚔, the action still happens, but a mishap strikes (see Settlement Mishaps).

Trigger: When your settlement wants to expand into a neighboring hex. Cost: One Season of attention and resources. Commitment: 5 families for the Season. Outcome: The hex becomes Claimed at Control 1.
You must have access to the hex (by travel or road) and a reason to hold it (food, material, defense, or trade). Claims can only be made in adjacent hexes unless a road or river link exists.
Claims require a visible presence: boundary markers, a seasonal camp, or routine patrol paths. If no one returns to a claimed hex during the Season, it cannot increase in Control.

When a territory action suffers a mishap, roll D66 and resolve the result. On a failed SETTLEMENT roll, D3 committed families lose their sole provider and count as one-third of a family until the end of the next Season.

rows: Bitter locals:Resentment simmers; Control does not increase next Season.
Wounded workers:A key crew is hurt; reduce output by one step next Season.
Lost supplies:The next Improvement costs +1 resource unit.
Tools break:Progress slows; halve yield in this hex for one Season.
Bad omens:The nextControl Checkin this hex suffers -1 die.
Camp sickness:One committed family is sidelined until next Season.
Petty theft:Stores are light; lose 1 resource unit.
Delayed labor:Work finishes late; reduce Control by 1 in this hex for one Season.
Strained ties:A neighboring settlement grumbles; -1 on the next negotiation roll with them.
Short rations:The crew eats the surplus; reduce Food yield by 25% this Season.
Blunt weather:A storm ruins a week of work; reduce output by one step next Season.
Unpaid hands:Wages or shares fall short; lose 1 committed family next Season.
Hidden danger:A lair or hazard is uncovered; the hex cannot be developed until it is cleared.
Border skirmish:Rival scouts clash; lose 1 Control in this hex.
Wild beasts:Predators scatter livestock; Pasture/Sheepfold yield is halved this Season.
Rot or rust:Stored inputs spoil; the next Improvement costs +1 resource unit.
False claim:Old markers are challenged; you must patrol next Season or lose 1 Control.
Bridge out:A road link becomes a trail until repaired.
Sabotage:Someone damages works; pay 1 resource unit or lose 1 Control.
Poached ground:Outsiders take the best spots; yield is halved this Season.
Missing tools:The crew wastes time; increase families needed by +1 next Season.
Fire in camp:Lose 1 resource unit and reduce output by one step next Season.
Unrest:A dispute turns violent; Control does not increase next Season.
Minor raid:The hex is raided; lose 1 Control unless patrols were assigned.
Hard winter:A blight or frost hits; Food yields -25% next Season.
Bandit toll:Pay 2 silver or lose 1 Control and 1 resource unit.
Broken morale:The crew deserts; action must be repeated next Season.
Collapsed works:A wall or tower fails; raise it again with half the materials.
Rival claim:A neighboring power marks the hex; it becomesContestedat Control 1.
Blood price:The settlement must pay 1 silver per Family or lose the claim.
Plague camp:D3 families are reduced to one-third until the end of next Season.
Major raid:Lose 2 Control; patrols reduce this to 1.
Disaster:A flood, fire, or cave-in destroys the Improvement; rebuild from scratch.
Supply crisis:Lose 3 resource units or the action fails.
Open revolt:The hex turns hostile; Control drops to 0 and it becomesWild.
War spark:A wider conflict ignites; the hex becomesContestedand both sides rollControl Checksnext Season.

segments.html: Control Score is adjusted by actions, improvements, and events. It governs safety, yields, and resistance.
Control Effects

rows: Wild. No yields. Encounters are common.
Developed. Full yields. Raids are rare.

Fortified. Full yields. Patrols deter most threats and land shows it. Paths are cut, markers stand, and locals know which banner is carried there. In a home hex, Ramparts, Guard Tower, and Portcullis set the practical ceiling for holding Control 5-6.

segments.html:
• +1 per Watchtower or Outpost.
  • +1 per Season of Patrols (see below).
  • +1 if a Road connects the hex to the stronghold.
  • -1 for a major raid or a successful enemy incursion.
  • -1 each Season the hex goes without upkeep.

• +1 per Season of Patrols (see below).

• -1 for a major raid or a successful enemy incursion.

segments.html: Trigger: When you invest in permanent use of the land. Cost: One Improvement and one Season. Commitment: 10 families per Improvement for the Season. Outcome: The hex becomes Developed and yields resources.

Improvements define what a hex produces and how it defends itself. Each developed hex can hold up to two Improvements without strain. A third Improvement requires the hex to be connected by road or river and increases upkeep by 1 resource unit per Season.

rows: Cows and a Herder or Fence; Barn required to feed cattle through Winter.

segments.html: Each developed hex yields resources once per Season. Base yields are derived from the stronghold function outputs and assume one full-time worker team (one family or one hireling) assigned to the hex for the full Season. A hex can only yield one primary resource per Season. If you assign additional families to the same hex, multiply the base yield per extra team.

Seasonal yields assume the settlement can spare the labor. Short seasons, raids, or shortages can cut yields even when the land is good. Round down fractions. Raw yields like milk, meat, and fish still require the same conversion functions as the stronghold rules (Dairy, Inn, Smokery) to become durable FOOD.

rows: Requires Farmer and a Plough. Oast House allows tobacco instead.
Requires Farmer and a Plough. Herbalist can swap herbs.
Requires cows and a Herder or Fence. Barn required to feed cattle through Winter. Up to 12 cows = 1008 milk/Season. Milk spoils daily; Dairy/Chef can convert to Food.
Pier doubles output; without it, use the base yield.
Requires a Plough and a Herbalist.

• Plains: Food +25%.
  • Forest/Dark Forest: Wood +25%.
  • Mountains: Stone +25%, Ore +25%.
  • Marshlands: Food -25%, Herbs +25%.
  • Ruins: Stone +25% (only once per Season).

• Summer: Food +25%.
  • Winter: Food -25%, Travel -1.

segments.html: To keep management simple, treat all hex yields as Seasonal totals. Use this cadence to map Quarter Days and days into Seasonal output:

• One Season equals three months (twelve weeks).
  • A single Quarter Day of work in a hex counts as 1/48 of a Season.
  • A full day of work counts as 1/24 of a Season.
  • A full week of work counts as 1/12 of a Season.
itemLiHtmls: • One Season equals three months (twelve weeks).
• A single Quarter Day of work in a hex counts as 1/48 of a Season.
• A full day of work counts as 1/24 of a Season.
• A full week of work counts as 1/12 of a Season.

segments.html: If you want to track partial Season work, divide the Seasonal yield by the fraction of work completed. Example: two weeks of mining is 2/12 of the Season yield.

Trigger: When you want to connect two adjacent hexes by road. Cost: One Season of work and materials per the Road function. Commitment: 8 families for the Season (4 families to repair from trail). Outcome: A road is drawn between the hexes. Each connected hex gains +1 Control, development can extend along a chain of roads, and travel speed increases by +1 hex per Quarter Day along roaded hexes.

Roads are marked on the map as a crude line between two bordering hex centers. If a road sees no traffic or maintenance for a Season, treat it as a trail until repaired by half the Families needed to establish it.

Trigger: When you want a permanent garrison point in a claimed or developed hex. Cost: One Season of work and materials for the structure. Commitment: 6 families for the Season. Outcome: The hex gains a Watchtower or Outpost Improvement and +1 Control.
Patrols keep roads open, intercept raiders, and stabilize claims.

Trigger: When you assign defenders to a hex for a Season. Cost: One unit of Food per 10 defenders per Season. Effect: +1 Control for that Season. Patrols also grant +2 dice to Control Checks against raids.
Patrols draw on the same pool of able hands used for field work and construction. Heavy patrol seasons slow development.

When a hex is threatened or contested, roll Control Checks. If two or more sides commit in the same Season over the same hex, the checks are opposed: all sides roll, the side with the most successes wins, and ties leave Control unchanged.
Test: Roll a number of dice equal to Control Score + local advantages. Success: The settlement holds the hex. Failure: Control drops by 1 and the enemy gains a foothold.
Local advantages include watchtowers, outposts, shrine bonus, and patrols.

When two settlements claim the same hex, it becomes Contested. Each Season, both sides roll a Control Check. The winner may increase Control by 1; the loser decreases by 1. If a side reaches Control 0, it loses the claim.
Conflicts over territory are resolved by seasons, not battles alone.
Skirmish Season: Each side rolls a Control Check. The winner may:

• Push a claim into a neighboring hex, or
  • Reduce enemy Control in a contested hex by 1, or
  • Break a road link for one Season.
itemLiHtmls: • Push a claim into a neighboring hex, or
• Reduce enemy Control in a contested hex by 1, or
• Break a road link for one Season.

segments.html: War Season: If both sides commit, each rolls two Control Checks and applies both results. A third party can intervene by claiming a contested hex at Control 1.

When a settlement is weakened, nearby wild forces press in. If a settlement loses Control in its home hex, the stronghold is under siege in all but name. Apply -2 to all MAKE CAMP and LEAD THE WAY rolls within two hexes until Control is restored.
Each developed hex that produces Food supports settlement growth. For every two developed Food hexes connected by road or river, the settlement may add one Family per Year if it is safe and supplied.

The stronghold claims a Forest hex, succeeds, and builds a Lumber Camp. It gains Control 2 after a watchtower is raised and patrols are assigned. The next Season it links a road and develops a second Improvement, pushing Control to 4. The border becomes reliable, and the settlement can expand toward a river.

Treat Control as the settlement’s visible pulse. A quiet Season with steady patrols, mended roads, and stocked stores reads like a living place; a frayed Season smells of smoke and rumor. Use Control shifts to signal the world’s mood: a drop means fences sag, trails grow meaner, and old threats start to drift back toward the hearth. When players return to a border they thought was safe, describe the small signs first—fresh cuts in bark, a missing shrine ribbon, a smoke plume that should not be there—then let the mechanics confirm what they already feel in their bones.

Keep the Season cadence as a story clock, not a ledger. Let the span of three months breathe: there is time for hard labor, slow trade, and quiet feuds to set roots. When a hex develops, describe how the land changes in texture—the furrowed field, the cleared line through the forest, the quarry’s scar and the camp that grows around it. That steady rhythm makes setbacks meaningful and recoveries earned, and it gives your campaign a sense of history written in the landscape rather than in a single roll.

Let territory be a stage for relationships, not just resources. A claimed hex might be marked by banners and argument, while a developed hex is held by habits and loyalties. Settlers argue over grazing, foresters grumble when the road eats their hunting ground, and neighboring clans test the edges of your authority. Give each hex a small identity—a name, a keeper, a grudge—and your players will see their stronghold as a living polity. The rules become a lens for politics, culture, and ambition, which is where the best long-term play grows.

Iron does not announce itself. Stone and clay show themselves to a trained eye, but ore veins run blind beneath the surface. The old miners of Harga knew the signs — color in a streambed, a certain weight in the soil, the way a hillside sheds water after rain. You must learn the same, or pay someone who already has.

A stronghold devours raw materials. Walls want stone. Roofs want timber. Forges want iron. The land holds all of these — but not in every hex, not in equal measure, and not forever. Before you can build, you must find what the earth is willing to give. Before you can dig, you must know where to put the pick.
This section covers how to discover natural resources in a hex, how to extract them, how fast they run out, and how to move them to where they are needed.
Prospecting is the act of surveying a hex for exploitable natural resources. It is a Quarter Day activity. You must be present in the hex.

Roll: SCOUTING (for surface resources: timber, stone, clay, peat, sand) or SURVIVAL (for subsurface resources: iron ore, silver ore, gold, bog iron). Add terrain modifiers from the Prospecting Modifiers table below. A character with the PATHFINDER talent adds +1. A character with the BUILDER talent adds +1 when prospecting for stone or ore.

Each hex may be prospected once per resource category per visit. You cannot roll for iron, fail, and immediately try again. You must leave the hex and return — or spend a full day (two Quarter Days) conducting a deeper survey, which allows a second roll at -1.

Prospecting can be done during a journey. It follows the same Quarter Day rules as HIKE, FORAGE, HUNT, KEEP WATCH, REST, SLEEP, and MAKE CAMP. You cannot hike and prospect in the same Quarter Day — you must remain stationary in the hex. A party that wants to prospect a hex typically arrives by hiking in one Quarter Day, prospects in the second, and rests or camps in the third and fourth. If you are already camped in a hex, prospecting costs only the Quarter Day with no travel penalty.

rows: Nothing found. The hex may still contain resources — you simply failed to find them.
Common deposit found.The GM reveals one common resource present in the hex (stone, clay, sand, peat, timber — whichever fits the terrain). Roll the deposit die on the Deposit Size table.
Significant deposit found.As above, but the GM may reveal a less common resource (iron ore, bog iron, salt). Roll the deposit die with +1.
Rich deposit found.As above, plus the GM may reveal a rare resource (silver ore, gold, gemstone, marble, limestone). Roll the deposit die with +2.

segments.html: A hex can contain multiple deposits of different types. Each prospecting roll can reveal at most one. The GM decides which deposits exist based on terrain and setting — the table gives the player's roll a mechanical gateway, but the GM is never forced to place silver in a plains hex because a player rolled three sixes.

A successful prospecting roll for subsurface resources with 2+ successes that reveals iron or silver ore satisfies the MINE function's "minable resource found" prerequisite. A successful prospecting roll for surface resources with 1+ success that reveals stone, clay, sand, or peat satisfies the QUARRY function's resource prerequisite.

When a deposit is found, roll on this table to determine its scale. The deposit die represents the total extractable material. It is not rolled during extraction — it is degraded over time by exploitation (see Depletion).

rows: Pocket.A surface scatter, an exposed seam, a single fallen trunk. Enough for a few days of work.
Seam.A workable deposit. Enough to support a season of digging or cutting.
Vein.A substantial find. Enough to justify building a mine, quarry, or lumber camp.
Lode.A major deposit. Rare, valuable, and worth defending. Worth building a stronghold around.

segments.html: The approximate total yield is a guideline, not a tracked number. The deposit die handles depletion abstractly.

Each terrain type offers different resources. The GM may adjust entries for local fiction, but this table is the baseline. A resource marked Common can be found on a single prospecting success. One marked Uncommon requires two successes. One marked Rare requires three or more.
Salvage resources from Ruins are reclaimed, not mined. They count as half-weight for transport because they come pre-shaped but damaged.

A mine is not a hole. It is a throat driven into the earth, propped with beams that want to bow, drained of water that wants to rise, and fed with men who want to leave. Every unit of ore costs sweat, timber, and risk. If you think you can dig wealth from the ground the way you pick flowers from a meadow, the mountain will teach you otherwise.
Once a deposit has been found, it can be worked. Each method below is a Quarter Day activity. All yields assume one worker.

rows: Any hex with trees. No prospecting needed.
Requires tunnel supports (1 wood per QD). Collapse risk.
Panning (rivers) uses SURVIVAL. Mining uses MIGHT.
Seasonal: available Spring and Fall only.

segments.html: Multiple workers in the same deposit multiply yield linearly, up to the capacity of the operation. A MINE or QUARRY function supports up to twelve workers. Without a built function, no more than four workers can operate at once — the tunnel or pit is simply too cramped.

A lone adventurer with a pickaxe can dig ore from a found deposit at the field rate above. Building a MINE, QUARRY, or LUMBER CAMP increases throughput, adds hireling capacity, and unlocks seasonal batch yields. The field rates exist so that a party on the road can work a deposit without building permanent infrastructure.

Underground mining carries collapse risk. For each week of underground mining, roll one Gear Die. On a 💀, a tunnel section collapses. Roll another Gear Die for each worker inside — another 💀 means that worker is trapped. Trapped NPCs are killed. A trapped PC suffers an attack of ten Base Dice (Weapon Damage 1, blunt force). If the PC survives, they must make a MIGHT roll to dig free or wait for rescue.

Surface quarrying, timber felling, panning, and open-air digging carry no collapse risk — but they carry weather risk. Work in rain, storm, or cold imposes the same penalties as hiking in those conditions (Chapter 8).

The dwarves of Moldena speak of a mine's life the way a druid speaks of a tree's. It is born when the first pick breaks stone. It grows when the veins branch. It sickens when the ore thins to dust and the water rises. And it dies when the last man walks out and the mountain closes behind him. Every mine dies. The question is how much it gives before it does.
Every deposit has a deposit die assigned when it is discovered. The deposit die is not rolled to produce material — it is rolled to check whether exploitation has begun to exhaust the source.
Depletion roll: At the end of each Season (three months) of active exploitation, roll the deposit die once. On a 1, the deposit die degrades one step:
D12 → D10 → D8 → D6 → Exhausted
When a D6 deposit rolls a 1, the deposit is exhausted. No further material can be extracted.
Heavy exploitation accelerates depletion. If more than six workers operated in the deposit during the Season, roll the depletion die twice and apply the worse result.

Intermittent use slows depletion. If the deposit was worked for fewer than four weeks of the Season, skip the depletion roll entirely. This rewards careful, seasonal extraction — the old pattern of working a mine in summer and leaving it to drain in winter.
Mineral deposits — stone, ore, silver, gold — do not recover. Once exhausted, they are gone. The mountain gave what it had.

Timber recovers. If a forested hex is not logged for two full Seasons (six months), roll a D6. On a 5–6, the deposit die recovers one step (minimum D6). Coppiced woodland — timber cut above the root so the stump resprouts — recovers on a 4–6. A character with the HERBALIST talent or a druid can supervise coppicing.
Peat recovers very slowly. If a peat deposit is not cut for one full year, roll a D6. On a 6, the deposit die recovers one step.

Bog iron recovers seasonally. Bog iron forms in waterlogged soil through natural processes. A depleted bog iron deposit recovers one die step per year automatically, without a roll, as long as the marshland hex is not drained or built over.

Clay and sand do not deplete under normal use. A clay or sand deposit is effectively inexhaustible at the scale of play. Do not track a deposit die for these materials unless something specific happens — a flood buries the clay pit, a landslide covers the sand bank.
Raw materials are heavy. Moving them from the deposit to the stronghold is a logistical problem, not a footnote.

rows: Requires a cart or dragging. Cannot be carried in a backpack.
Requires a cart. Wagons cannot enter difficult terrain.
Bulky but light. Sacks or barrels.
Lighter than raw timber; requires a SAWMILL to produce.
Very light. Fragile. Crumbles if dropped or rained on.

segments.html: Cart capacity: A cart drawn by one horse carries 50 weight-units of material. A wagon drawn by two horses carries 100. Neither can enter difficult terrain unless a ROAD exists.

River transport: If the source hex connects to the stronghold hex by river, timber can be floated downstream at no cart cost. One worker per 20 units of timber manages the float. Stone and ore cannot be floated.
Road bonus: If a ROAD connects the two hexes, transport time is halved and wagon capacity doubles for that route.

The distance in hexes between deposit and stronghold determines transport time: one Quarter Day per hex of open terrain, two per hex of difficult terrain. A round trip doubles the time. Building roads, bridges, and river piers is the answer to transport cost — and always has been.

segments.text: STONE SONG AND THE DEEP EARTH

segments.html: Before the Blood Mist, the dwarves did not mine with picks. They sang — a low guttural drone pressed against the living rock that made the stone answer, revealing its veins and yielding along its grain. That art is nearly dead. Stone Song (Chapter 7) is the rarest magical tradition in the Forbidden Lands. Most outsiders never learn beyond rank 1. Rank 3 and above remain within the clans. If your band has no stone singer, nothing in these rules requires one.
A stone singer who casts Voice of the Mountain (rank 1 ritual) while prospecting does not roll SCOUTING or SURVIVAL. The mountain answers directly.

• Power Level 1: Confirms a deposit exists in the hex. Does not reveal type or size. Equivalent to 1 prospecting success.
  • Power Level 2: Reveals type and approximate location of one deposit. Equivalent to 2 successes.
  • Power Level 3: Reveals all deposits in the hex, their types, and approximate sizes. Equivalent to 3+ successes. Roll deposit dice for each.
itemLiHtmls: • Power Level 1: Confirms a deposit exists in the hex. Does not reveal type or size. Equivalent to 1 prospecting success.
• Power Level 2: Reveals type and approximate location of one deposit. Equivalent to 2 successes.
• Power Level 3: Reveals all deposits in the hex, their types, and approximate sizes. Equivalent to 3+ successes. Roll deposit dice for each.

segments.html: The ritual costs one Quarter Day — the same as a normal prospecting roll — but cannot fail.

Feel the Vibrations (rank 2) is faster: one turn instead of a Quarter Day. It grants +2 to a subsurface prospecting roll rather than replacing it. The singer senses density changes — voids, metal seams, water pockets — but must still interpret what they mean.

A stone singer at the rock face changes the nature of the work entirely. The singer does not swing a pick — the singer works the stone with voice and vibration while the crew handles loosened material.

• Stonesmith (rank 2 ritual): Creates tunnel supports from the surrounding rock itself. No timber required. Eliminates the 1-wood-per-QD support cost for the duration.
  • Shape the Stone (rank 2): Softens the seam face so the crew can pull material free by hand. Doubles extraction yield for one Quarter Day per Power Level.
  • Iron Song (rank 3 ritual): Draws pure iron from raw ore by voice, bypassing smelting. One casting processes Power Level × 10 units of ore. Requires a forge and raw ore on hand.
  • Way of the Mountain (rank 5): Perfect awareness of tunnels, caves, and fault lines in the hex. While active, collapse risk is eliminated — the singer knows where every weakness lies and steers the crew clear.
  • Petrify (rank 3): Turns wood to stone or hardens soft ground into load-bearing rock. Used to seal flood-prone tunnels or convert timber bracing into permanent stone pillars.

• Iron Song (rank 3 ritual): Draws pure iron from raw ore by voice, bypassing smelting. One casting processes Power Level × 10 units of ore. Requires a forge and raw ore on hand.

• Petrify (rank 3): Turns wood to stone or hardens soft ground into load-bearing rock. Used to seal flood-prone tunnels or convert timber bracing into permanent stone pillars.

segments.html: Before the Blood Mist, dwarven mining was choral work. The old delvings beneath Hagha Ard and the silver road of Belderek were opened by organized voices, not tools. When stone singers work together, they add Power Levels to the lead singer's spell. Each supporting singer must know the spell (at any rank) and spend a fast action harmonizing.
Supporting singers pay no WP. The bonus cannot exceed +3.

A quartet casting Voice of the Mountain at effective Power Level 3+ also reveals whether adjacent hexes contain significant deposits — the GM answers yes or no per hex, no further detail. A chamber chorus or grand chorus casting Shape the Stone or Stonesmith triples extraction yield for the Quarter Day instead of doubling it. A grand chorus mine produces no noise at all — only a low vibration felt through the soles of the feet on the surface above.

Assembling a quartet of stone singers is an extraordinary event in the current age. A chamber chorus has not gathered since before the Blood Mist. A grand chorus belongs to the age of legends, when the dwarves raised mountains for their god Huge.

"Oil is well and all, but nothing beats the spit of a ginger girl for a better grip!" Haggamur mused, as he dipped the cloth and greased his axe with it by the campfire in the night. "Like any girl ever let you close!" Molder said from the fire. "But he does know everything about a good grip on his shaft," laughed Miria Mott.
The following tables cover various kinds of goods and services available in the Forbidden Lands.

Some goods and services are rare and the adventurers can't expect to find everything they're looking for in any little village. Each item lists a Supply rating, which indicates the probability that the adventurers will find the item in a typical village.
COMMON: The item is generally available in decent quantities.
UNCOMMON: Roll a D6. If the result is 4 or higher, one D6 units of the item are available. A new roll can be made each week.
RARE: Roll a D6. The item is available on a 6 only, and only one item is available. A new roll can be made once every week.
EXTREMELY RARE: Roll a D66. The item is available on 65-66 only, and only one item is available. A new roll can be made once every week.
Markets in the Ravenlands run like early medieval exchanges: local, personal, and shaped by scarcity more than coin.

• Gold is ceremonial: Gold prices mark prestige and patronage, not daily trade. In villages, gold-priced items require a sponsor, a special order, or a rare caravan; if purchased locally, treat the item as Extremely Rare and add 1D6 weeks lead time.
  • Silver and barter dominate: Use silver and copper for daily goods. If a price feels too high for a village, allow barter at face value or substitute a service obligation.
  • Scarcity inflation: If an item is Rare or Extremely Rare and actually found, increase the price by 50% to 200% based on local need.

segments.html: • Specialist access: Items that require advanced talents (smith, bowyer, builder) may be unavailable outside towns or strongholds even if the supply roll succeeds.

segments.html: Most of the items in the gear lists can be made using the crafting skill.
RAW MATERIALS: This column indicates the raw materials needed to craft the item. Raw materials can, in some cases, be other items. If no raw materials are listed, the item cannot be crafted.

TIME: The gear tables also list how long it takes to craft the item, assuming the artisan works for two Quarter Days per day. If additional time is spent on the work, the artisan gets a bonus to their roll.

TALENTS: Items are classified as advanced if they require a specific talent to be crafted. This is indicated in the Talent column. If no talent is listed, the item is simple and can be crafted by anyone.

TOOLS: Many items require specific tools to be crafted. Such requirements are listed in the Tools column. Some items even require certain functions, such as a forge, to be made. Read more about functions in Chapter 9. Functions don’t only exist in strongholds – the adventurers can find them in villages and other locations in the Forbidden Lands as well.
In the Forbidden Lands workshops are scarce, skilled labor is uneven, and time is the true price.
WORKSHOP LIMITS: If the required function or tool set is missing, increase crafting time by 50% and apply -1 to the roll.
SPECIALISTS: Advanced items require a specialist. If none is present, crafting is impossible without training or outside help.
ASSISTANTS: Large items (armor, crossbows, vehicles) require at least one assistant. Each assistant beyond the first reduces time by 25%, to a minimum of half the listed time with three assistants.
FITTING TIME: Armor requires 1-2 extra days of fitting. Poor fit gives -1 to MOVE or -1 Armor Rating until adjusted.
SEASONAL WORK: Outdoor or heavy craft slows in winter; increase time by 50% unless indoors with proper functions.

segments.html: Rope and Textile Quality: When purchasing rope, cloth, tents, or clothing, choose a quality tier that affects lifespan, not performance.

• Rough: Half lifespan in harsh use; cost -25%.
  • Standard: Use the table price and lifespan.
  • Fine: Double lifespan; cost +50%. Requires a skilled maker.

• Standard: Use the table price and lifespan.
• Fine: Double lifespan; cost +50%. Requires a skilled maker.

segments.html: If a skill roll leans on rope or cloth and really strains it (a hard climb, yanking a tent seam), check for wear by quality:

• Rough: Damaged on two 💀 (no bonus until repaired); Tears on 3+ 💀.
  • Standard: Damaged on 3+ 💀 (no bonus until repaired).
  • Fine: It doesn’t wear out from normal strain during its lifespan unless someone cuts it on purpose; when rope is damaged, 1 damage only damages it, and 2 and more damage tears it.
